source.title: Successor Heads: Recurring, Interpretable Attention Heads In The Wild
source.authors: Rhys Gould; Euan Ong; George Ogden; Arthur Conmy

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses whether individual neurons can be interpretable, and reports neuron experiments on a narrow numeric task, but it does not test any listed claim version about audit shares, other-model shares, InceptionV1, attribution graphs, or explanation scoring.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that individual MLP0 neurons important for numeric succession show periodic firing patterns, but gives no audit of neuron poles or estimates of how many have one or more jobs. Its successor-head scores across models and its natural-text head-ablation results concern attention heads, not the listed neuron-audit claims, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper is about successor attention heads. Its only neuron result covers the 16 MLP0 neurons of Pythia-1.4B that matter most for numeric succession, chosen by ablation. It reports no share of neurons or poles with one or more jobs, and no study of InceptionV1. It builds no attribution graphs and does not score neuron explanations. It mentions neuron interpretability only to set its narrow result against Elhage et al. (2022), so it discusses the claim without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate but narrow. The main conclusion is that successor heads recur across models from 31M to 12B parameters and use shared mod-10 features, a weak form of universality. The authors call the individual MLP0 neurons 'surprisingly interpretable' on this narrow task. They say this does not contradict evidence that MLP behaviour is distributed, since f6 appears in superposition across neurons. They also find the successor head is interpretably polysemantic (succession plus acronyms).
record.recipe_differences: No method for auditing neuron-pole job counts is tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Of the 16 MLP0 neurons in Pythia-1.4B most important for succession, the most common firing period is 10. Several fire on a single residue mod 10, while the f6 feature is spread across at least two neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Pythia-1.4B, the MLP0 neurons most important for numeric succession often fire in clean mod-10 patterns, though some features are split across neurons. No population share is given.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention head L12H0 is interpretably polysemantic. Across winning cases, its behaviour splits into successorship 43.4%, acronym 23.8% and greater-than 18.9%. These are related ordinal-and-letter jobs inside one component, but the component is an attention head, not a neuron.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some LLM attention heads do a few distinct but interpretable jobs (interpretable polysemanticity). This bears loosely on the 'two related jobs' category, but for heads rather than neurons.

record.problems: The neuron experiments focus on a single model and a narrow numeric-succession task. The top 16 neurons are selected for their ablation impact, and the text gives no numerical ablation probabilities or population-level estimate of neuron interpretability.
record.rows_left_out: Successor-head measurements across models and head-ablation results on natural-language contexts are not rows because they do not measure the neuron-job claims. Other neuron-feature results, including mod-10 feature transfer and linear probing, do not report neuron-pole job shares.

untested.parts: All parts: no audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or their job shares.
All parts: successor heads are compared across models, but no neuron-job shares are given for any model.
All parts: no InceptionV1 or cat-and-car neuron, and no test of recursive generalization versus superposition for neurons.
All parts: no interpretable-neuron shares compared across architectures or tools.
All parts: no neuron-based attribution graphs.
All parts: no test of whether explanations drawn from activating examples predict where a neuron fires.
All parts: no simulation-based scoring of explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The neuron analysis covers one model, one layer (MLP0) and 16 neurons chosen for their task impact, so it cannot speak to the share of neurons with one main job. The reader's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are kept.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not count neuron poles by number of jobs or report shares that are understood, have one main job, or have multiple jobs.
It reports successor heads across models, but does not audit neuron-job shares across models, architectures, or scales.
It does not study InceptionV1 or the cat-and-car example.
It does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares across architectures or tools.
It does not build or evaluate attribution graphs.
It does not test whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire.
It does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Pythia-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated individual MLP0 neurons and measured the probability assigned to the successor of numeric tokens.

conditions.value: individual MLP0 neurons; top 16 ranked by impact on successor probability

rows.value: The authors identify neurons with the lowest averaged correct successor probability after ablation as having the greatest impact; numerical probabilities are not reported in the text.
rows.note: The top 16 neurons were selected by this ablation-based measure; the paper does not report a neuron-job audit or prevalence.
rows.check: This is a selection step rather than a result. Ablation is used only to rank and pick the top 16 neurons, and no probabilities are reported. It should be folded into R2's condition or dropped as a row.

rows.subject: Pythia-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Examined firing intensities of the MLP0 neurons identified as important for numeric succession across number-token inputs.
rows.measure: Periodic pattern in neuron firing intensity
rows.value: The authors report periodic spiking patterns; the most common period among the top 16 neurons is 10.
rows.note: The paper states that some neurons show modulo-10 patterns and that feature f6 appears to be distributed across at least two neurons. This is a narrow-task result, not a count of poles with one main job.
rows.check: Linking to none is correct. Periodic (mod-10) firing in 16 hand-picked, task-selected neurons says nothing about what share of a model's neurons have one main job. The authors also note that f6 is spread across at least two neurons. The numbers_found value '2/2' is meaningless and should be cleared.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
